title: Leaders Who Need to Turn Off Their Relentless Focus
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article applies the concept of hypervigilance, usually associated with law enforcement and military professionals, to highly driven leaders who can never fully switch off their scanning, evaluating minds. It describes how this constant state of assessment brings energy and insight to every conversation but also exhausts the leader and strains their relationships. Rather than adding another demanding activity as a distraction, which risks becoming just another arena for hypervigilance, the piece recommends genuinely disengaging practices like meditation and yoga. It closes by framing the ability to turn off as a real and underappreciated leadership challenge worth confronting directly.
points: Highly driven leaders can become hypervigilant, unable to relax even when 'off duty.'
Hypervigilance brings energy and insight to conversations but leads to exhaustion and strained relationships.
Adding another demanding activity as a distraction often just creates a new arena for hypervigilance.
Genuine disengagement, through practices like meditation or yoga, is a better antidote.
Teaching hypervigilant leaders to relax can meaningfully improve their long-term wellbeing.
quotes: Leaders who are highly driven to learn and excel sometimes can become hypervigilant about everything in their world.
Those who maintain a never-ending level of awareness and arousal often have a difficult time relaxing even when they are “off duty.
It is no surprise that leaders who are hypervigilant have difficulty maintaining relationships and often experience severe mental health issues.
If they can’t turn off and enjoy themselves, they can be especially difficult to work or live with.
Better is to push these leaders to meditation, yoga, and experiences that require complete disengagement and provide a connection to other people.
Who knew that, for some leaders, turning off is the biggest challenge they face?
